questions.knowledge_point: Finding Critical Points of Polynomials
questions.problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)={x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}+21x+23.$
questions.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}+12{x}^{2}+21x+23) \\  & =3{x}^{2}+24x+21.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}+24x+21 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+8x+7 & =0 \\ (x+1)(x+7) & =0 \\ x & =-1,\,-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-1$ and $x=-7.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-1$ and $x=-7.$

questions.problem: Find the critical points of the function  $f(x)=({x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}){e}^{4{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(({x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}){e}^{4{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={({x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4})}^{′}{e}^{4{x}^{2}}+({x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}){({e}^{4{x}^{2}})}^{′} \\  & =2x{e}^{4{x}^{2}}+(8x)({x}^{2}-\frac{5}{4}){e}^{4{x}^{2}} \\  & =[2x+8{x}^{3}-10x]{e}^{4{x}^{2}} \\  & =(8{x}^{3}-8x){e}^{4{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(8{x}^{3}-8x){e}^{4{x}^{2}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${e}^{4{x}^{2}}\ne 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by ${e}^{4{x}^{2}}$ and solve the resulting equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}8{x}^{3}-8x & =0 \\ 8x({x}^{2}-1) & =0 \\ 8x(x+1)(x-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\,-1,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-1,$ $x=0$ and $x=1.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=-1,$ $x=0$ and $x=1.$

questions.problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x)=\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}-2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{2x-3}{{x}^{2}-2}) \\  & =\frac{(2x-3)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)-(2x-3)\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)^{′}}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot ({x}^{2}-2)-(2x-3)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-4+6x-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{2{x}^{2}-6x+4}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where ${f}^{′}(c)=0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{2{x}^{2}-6x+4}{({x}^{2}-2)^{2}} & =0 \\ 2{x}^{2}-6x+4 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-3x+2 & =0 \\ (x-1)(x-2) & =0 \\ x & =1,\,2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=1$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ does not exist at $x=\pm \sqrt{2}.$ But these points do not lie in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=1$ and $x=2.$

$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=-2$ and $x=2.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

$$

A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either ${f}^{′}(c)=0$ or ${f}^{′}(c)$ does not exist.

$$

$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+n\pi  \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We set $n=0,\pm 1,\pm 2,…,$ until we have generated all solutions in the domain $0<x<2\pi .$

- setting $n=0$ gives $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$

- setting $n=1$ gives $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}$

All other values of $n$ generate solutions outside the domain $0<x<2\pi .$ So, the solutions to this equation for $x\in (0,2\pi )$ are 

$$
x=\frac{\pi }{4},\,x=\frac{5\pi }{4}.
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

- Second, we note that ${f}^{′}(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in (0,2\pi ).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in (0,2\pi )$ are ${x}_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${x}_{2}=\frac{5\pi }{4}.$

Finally,

$$
{x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot \frac{5\pi }{4}=\frac{5{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x)=2x^3-3x^2+5.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+5) \\  & =6{x}^{2}-6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-6x & =0 \\ 6x(x-1) & =0 \\ x=0,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=0$ and $x=1.$

- Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=0$ and $x=1.$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the critical points of the function $f(x) = e^{x^3-x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({e}^{{x}^{3}-x}) \\  & ={({x}^{3}-x)}^{′}{e}^{{x}^{3}-x} \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-1){e}^{{x}^{3}-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{x}^{2}-1){e}^{{x}^{3}-x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $e^{x^3-x} \neq 0$ for all $x,$ we can divide this equation by $e^{x^3-x}$ and solve the resulting equation. 

$$
\begin{aligned}(3{x}^{2}-1){e}^{{x}^{3}-x} & =0 \\ 3{x}^{2}-1 & =0 \\ x & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}$ and $x=-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}.$

- Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x$ in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}$ and $x=-\dfrac{\sqrt 3}{3}.$

canonical_examples.problem: What are the critical points of the function $f(x) = \dfrac {x-3}{x^2 -6}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
A critical point of $f(x)$ is a point $x=c$ in the domain of $f$ such that either $f'(c)=0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist.

Differentiating $f(x),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{x-3}{{x}^{2}-6}) \\  & =\frac{(x-3)^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}-6)-(x-3)\cdot ({x}^{2}-6)^{′}}{({x}^{2}-6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}-6)-(x-3)\cdot 2x}{({x}^{2}-6)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-6+6x-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}-6)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+6}{({x}^{2}-6)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x$ by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{{x}^{2}-6x+6}{({x}^{2}-6)^{2}} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-6x+6 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+6 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-9+6 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2}-3 & =0 \\ (x-3)^{2} & =3 \\ x-3 & =\pm \sqrt{3} \\ x & =3\pm \sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)$ has stationary points at $x=3\pm \sqrt 3.$

- Second, we note that $f'(x)$ does not exist at $x=\pm \sqrt 6.$ But these points do not lie in the domain of $f(x).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ are $x=3\pm \sqrt 3.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We now proceed to find the critical points:

- First, we compute the points where $f'(c) = 0.$ We set the derivative equal to zero, and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =0 \\ 2\operatorname{sin}⁡2x & =-2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} & =-\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{2}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡2x} \\ \operatorname{tan}⁡2x & =-\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(-\sqrt{3})+n\pi  \\ 2x & =-\frac{\pi }{3}+n\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
x =-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \qquad x =  \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
$$

- Second, we note that $f'(x)$ exists for all values of $x\in \left(-\dfrac\pi2, \dfrac\pi2\right).$ So $f(x)$ has no non-stationary critical points.

Therefore, we conclude that the critical points of $f(x)$ for $x\in \left(-\dfrac\pi2, \dfrac\pi2\right)$ are

$$
x_1 =-\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \qquad x_2 =  \dfrac{\pi}{3}.
